channel.title: Labour Law on Legal Winter
channel.description: Recent content in Labour Law on Legal Winter

item.title: Cross-border and international employment
item.description:
The labour market in Northwestern Switzerland is strongly shaped by the tri-border region and cross-border cooperation. For many companies, employees residing in Germany or France are as much a part of everyday business as internationally recruited professionals. This creates particular legal requirements when structuring employment relationships.

Cross-border employment issues regularly involve employment law, tax law and social security law. Which rules apply depends, among other factors, on the employee’s place of residence, place of work, the extent of work performed abroad and nationality. An arrangement suitable for an employee residing in Germany therefore cannot simply be applied to an employee residing in France.

item.title: Employment Contracts
item.description:
Under Swiss law, employment contracts are generally not subject to any particular formal requirements. Nevertheless, it is advisable to set out the essential rights and obligations in writing, clearly and in a manner tailored to the specific employment relationship. Careful contract drafting creates certainty for both parties and provides a reliable basis if differing interpretations arise at a later stage.

Many employment law disputes can be traced back to unclear, contradictory or incomplete agreements. Anyone entering into a new employment relationship should therefore consider not only salary, position and working hours, but also provisions on bonuses, overtime, holidays, notice periods, non-compete clauses, place of work and home office arrangements.

item.title: Employment references
item.description:
Employment references are among the most common issues in employment law. A purely linguistic review can nowadays usually be carried out with relatively little effort. The key issue, however, is not merely to identify problematic wording, but to ensure that justified amendments are actually accepted by the employer.

An employment reference must be truthful, complete and at the same time formulated in a favourable manner. In practice, disputes frequently arise over whether duties and responsibilities have been accurately described, performance has been appropriately recognised, or the reasons for departure and assessments of conduct have been correctly worded. In reviewing an employment reference, I consider not only its wording, but also your actual role, the history of the employment relationship and the changes that are important for your future career.

item.title: Exit negotiations
item.description:
The termination of an employment relationship often raises issues that cannot be adequately addressed by notice of termination alone. A termination or separation agreement can be beneficial for employees at all levels, particularly where financial claims, the circumstances of departure or future career prospects need to be settled on a binding basis.

Such negotiations may cover matters including severance payments, the termination date, garden leave, outstanding holiday and overtime entitlements, bonus claims, the employment reference, and internal and external communications regarding the departure. For executives and senior professionals, additional issues often include variable compensation, participation or incentive plans, and more complex contractual arrangements.

item.title: Gender equality and workplace discrimination
item.description:
Gender equality is a principle to which many readily subscribe and which companies are often keen to emphasise. Yet when it comes to concrete decisions – recruitment, promotion, pay, pregnancy or dealing with sexual harassment – the reality can sometimes look quite different. Precisely where equality has practical consequences, what seemed to be a matter of principle can surprisingly quickly become a secondary concern.

Equality in the workplace, however, is not a nice-to-have or merely a matter of good corporate culture. It is a legal right.

item.title: Social security law
item.description:
Social security law issues are often closely connected with employment relationships. At the same time, social security law is a distinct and complex field in which employment law, insurance law and medical assessments intersect. I have dealt with specialised issues in this area since my university studies, subsequently in an academic context and, for several years, as part of my legal practice.

I represent clients in particular in disputes concerning daily sickness allowance benefits, questions relating to the legal assessment of incapacity for work and illness, and matters involving benefits under Swiss disability insurance. Other areas of my practice include occupational pension matters, such as changes of pension fund in connection with a transfer of business, as well as the assessment and enforcement of insurance claims.

item.title: Workplace bullying
item.description:
Workplace bullying is among the most difficult forms of conflict in an employment relationship. On the one hand, the term is sometimes used too readily today to describe any treatment perceived as unfair or hurtful. On the other hand, many workplaces still lack sufficient awareness of systematic exclusion, humiliation or harassment. Both tendencies make an objective assessment more difficult.

Not every conflict, unjustified criticism or isolated inappropriate remark constitutes workplace bullying in legal terms. The decisive question is whether hostile conduct is repeated over an extended period and, taken as a whole, is directed against a particular person. Such a situation may engage the employer’s duty of care and can have significant legal implications in connection with a termination, illness or other employment-related claims.

item.title: Dismissals
item.description:
Under Swiss employment law, the principle of freedom of termination generally applies: both employees and employers may terminate an open-ended employment relationship, provided that the contractual or statutory notice periods are observed. There is no general requirement to state a reason for termination. Nevertheless, the circumstances in which notice is given can be highly relevant from a legal perspective.

A termination may, in particular, be abusive if it is intended to prevent legitimate claims arising from the employment relationship or is given because an employee has asserted such claims. Terminations relating to an employee’s age, following many years of service, or arising from a conflict in which the employer may not have adequately fulfilled its duty of care also require careful assessment. The specific circumstances and events leading up to the termination are always crucial.
